extracted.intended_audience: practitioners representing trademark applicants before the USPTO (trademark attorneys/agents), and USPTO disciplinary adjudicators
extracted.subtask_description: Evaluation of a trademark practitioner's compliance with USPTO Rules of Professional Conduct (RPC) in trademark filings, signatures, declarations, specimens, account use, and cooperation with OED investigations. Focuses on conduct standards the Office applies when assessing disciplinary violations (competence, diligence, candor, signatures, cooperation, etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Competence (37 C.F.R. § 11.101)
rubrics_metrics.description: A practitioner must provide competent representation, exercising the legal, scientific, and technical knowledge, skill, thoroughness and preparation reasonably necessary for the representation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Competence includes reviewing and understanding USPTO rules regarding certifications and declarations (e.g., 37 C.F.R. § 11.18), signature regulations, and specimen requirements. Failure to comprehend or exercise these requirements (e.g., presenting pre-dated declarations or altered specimens) demonstrates lack of competence. Examples/citations: In re Aquilla; discussion of §11.18; repeated presentation of declarations that predated associated Office Actions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diligence (37 C.F.R. § 11.103)
rubrics_metrics.description: A practitioner must act with reasonable diligence and promptness in representing a client, pursuing a matter despite personal inconvenience, and acting with commitment and dedication to the client's interests.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Diligence is breached by failing to adequately review filings, relying on rubber-stamp or copy/paste tactics to handle high volumes, or otherwise taking shortcuts that lead to mistakes. Examples: filing 40 responses with pre-signed declarations; failing to review specimens resulting in refusals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Duty of Candor to the Tribunal (37 C.F.R. § 11.303(a)(1), (a)(3), (d))
rubrics_metrics.description: A practitioner shall not knowingly make a false statement of fact or law to a tribunal or fail to correct a false statement; shall not offer evidence the practitioner knows to be false; and in ex parte proceedings must inform the tribunal of all material facts known to the practitioner.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: ‘Tribunal’ includes the USPTO. 'Knowingly' is defined in §11.1 and may be inferred from circumstances. Examples of violations: submitting declarations that could not support the asserted facts (pre-generated/declarations predating Office Actions or specimens), filing CAR forms containing false reasons for change of representation, allowing others to sign the practitioner's name, and certifying a reasonable inquiry into specimens when none was done. Remedial duties include correcting false statements and, if necessary, disclosure to the tribunal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dishonesty/Fraud/Deceit (37 C.F.R. § 11.804(c))
rubrics_metrics.description: RPC proscribe conduct involving dishonesty, fraud, deceit, or misrepresentation; dishonest conduct is characterized by lack of truth, honesty, or trustworthiness and fraud requires intent to deceive (or reckless state of mind equivalent to intent).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Dishonesty generally requires intent to deceive; negligent or inattentive conduct that results in false statements may violate candor rules but not necessarily §11.804(c). Discussion distinguishes sanctionable dishonesty from negligent misstatements (citing In re Lane, Swayze, Piccone). The record must show intent for a finding of dishonest conduct.

rubrics_metrics.name: Failure to Cooperate with Disciplinary Investigation (37 C.F.R. § 11.801(b))
rubrics_metrics.description: A practitioner has a duty to cooperate with OED disciplinary investigations and respond to requests for information and evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Non-response or partial response to RFIs is a violation. Example: practitioner failed to answer question 7.d. of the First RFI and failed to respond to the Third RFI despite evidence of receipt (emails not undeliverable and continued email use).

rubrics_metrics.name: Conduct Prejudicial to the Administration of Justice (37 C.F.R. § 11.804(d))
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioner conduct that prejudices the administration of justice is prohibited under the RPC.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Complaint alleges such prejudicial conduct based on the factual allegations (examples of prejudice are developed elsewhere in the record). Entry included as a distinct basis for discipline.

rubrics_metrics.name: USPTO Change-of-Representation and Signature Rules (37 C.F.R. §§ 2.17, 2.19, 2.193(e); TMEP §§ 604.03, 712.01)
rubrics_metrics.description: When an applicant initially represented by an attorney hires a different attorney from a different law firm, the new attorney can sign responses only after the applicant has signed and filed a revocation of the current attorney or a power/appointment of attorney for the new attorney, or the current attorney withdraws.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Non-Responsive Submissions will refuse to review responses not signed by a proper party. Examples: CAR forms improperly signed by a new attorney (Respondent) resulted in a Non-Responsive Submission and a Notice of Abandonment. Citations: 37 C.F.R. § 2.193(e)(2)(i), TMEP § 712.01, and related TMEP sections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Certification/Declaration Compliance (including 37 C.F.R. § 11.18)
rubrics_metrics.description: Declarations and certifications presented to the Office must support the factual representations made in the trademark documents; practitioners must ensure the factual accuracy and temporal relevance of declarations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Presenting pre-signed H-SIGN declarations executed before the Office Action or before the specimen existed fails to support the factual assertions and violates certification obligations. Examples: at least 40 H-SIGN declarations executed before the associated Office Actions; substitute specimens with declarations dated before specimens' existence; filing via TEAS using practitioner's USPTO.gov account where receipts were sent to practitioner's email address.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reasonable Pre-Filing Inquiry into Specimens and Evidence of Use
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioners must conduct an inquiry reasonable under the circumstances before presenting specimens or other evidence of use, confirming that specimens are genuine and reflect actual use in commerce.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reasonable inquiry includes reviewing tags on goods, confirming an Amazon/e-commerce listing actually exists (reviews, verifiable listing), and detecting digital alterations. Failure to do so can result in Office Actions/refusals (examples: two applications with allegedly fabricated Amazon screenshots and 27 applications refused for digitally altered images).

rubrics_metrics.name: Signature Methods and Monitoring (H-SIGN, DIRECT, TEAS) and Responsibility for Signatures
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioners must accurately represent how signatures are obtained, personally obtain signatures when required, or, if another obtains the signature, describe the process and monitor it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OED requested detailed explanation (RFI question 7.d.) about signature methods used, whether practitioner personally obtains signatures, how others obtain signatures, and how practitioner monitors the means. Examples of misuse: DIRECT signatures timestamped/geo-located inconsistently (multiple CAR forms signed within an hour from IP addresses in different countries), and instances where practitioner allowed others to affix her signature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account Sponsorship and Control of USPTO.gov Accounts and Email
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioners who sponsor USPTO.gov accounts or use email addresses in practice must control and monitor those accounts, ensure proper use, and review filing receipts sent to those addresses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Respondent sponsored accounts for non-practitioner assistants and used multiple email addresses (info@yshipr.com, tianzhuojingwen@haibu.com.cn, jeannie124@hotmail.com). Filing receipts for disputed filings were sent to info@yshipr.com; Respondent stated she checked those inboxes 'basically everyday,' supporting inference of knowledge. Allowing others to use an account or failing to monitor account activity can indicate lack of competence/diligence or knowledge of improper filings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Knowledge Standard: 'Knowingly' and Inference from Circumstances (37 C.F.R. § 11.1)
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Knowingly' means actual knowledge of the fact in question, and a person's knowledge may be inferred from the circumstances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Director may infer knowledge from facts such as regular checking of an email that received filing receipts, impossible signature timing/geo-location, or other indicia. For Candor violations, intent to deceive is not required; knowledge can be inferred to satisfy §11.303 elements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Remedial Duties When Becoming Aware of False Evidence (37 C.F.R. § 11.303(a)(3) guidance)
rubrics_metrics.description: If a practitioner, client, or witness has offered material evidence that the practitioner knows to be false, the practitioner shall take reasonable remedial measures, including, if necessary, disclosure to the tribunal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If evidence or declarations are known or reasonably believed to be false, the practitioner must refuse to offer such evidence and must correct previously submitted false statements; failure to take these measures violates the duty of candor. Example: the rule is invoked when declarations or specimens are discovered to be pre-generated or falsified.

rubrics_metrics.name: Office as a 'Tribunal' for Purposes of RPC Duties (37 C.F.R. § 11.1 and RPC commentary)
rubrics_metrics.description: For RPC purposes, the term 'tribunal' includes the USPTO; therefore duties of candor and related RPC obligations apply to interactions with USPTO examining attorneys and Office procedures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This clarifies that the duty of candor and disclosure obligations are owed directly to USPTO examiners; failure to treat the Office as a tribunal (e.g., by not disclosing material facts in ex parte proceedings) can constitute an RPC violation.
